activity_context.topic_title: Analyzing Slope Fields for Autonomous Differential Equations

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/e0da4ce40e23a44ddfd946b9a9bf00882ca0a83db8379c6492b58355772c6006.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14064933/assets/ddac2bab6fb72979e1142179dfb11792cc50044de545131139edfdeff9215e3c.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope field is zero along the lines $y=\pm 2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on these lines.

Of the given equations, the only two that satisfy this condition are

$$
{y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}=(2+y)(2-y)
$$

 
and

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4=(y+2)(y-2).
$$

- Second, the lines $y=\pm 2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-2$ | $-2<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the two remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}=(2+y)(2-y).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=4-{y}^{2}.$
